home.heroTitle: Healthy recipes for your little ones
home.subtitle: Discover trusted recipes matched to your child's age: from first tastes to full family meals.
home.guideSub: Short answers to parents' first questions.
home.disclaimer: General guidance only — ask your pediatrician for personalised advice.

items.a: Around 6 months: baby holds the head steady, sits with support and shows interest in food. Your pediatrician confirms the right moment.
Simple veggies (carrot, zucchini, sweet potato), one new food every 2–3 days, with smooth textures at first.
A few teaspoons a day is plenty at first; milk stays the main food until age one. Grow portions gradually, following appetite.
That's normal. Offer again in a few days without pressure — acceptance usually comes after 8–10 exposures.
Generally around 6 months, when your baby is developmentally ready.

items.q: How do I know my baby is ready?
items.a: Readiness signs include sitting with support, good head and neck control, and interest in foods.
Start with simple, age-appropriate foods: veggies, fruits, cereals, meat, egg and other nutritious foods, introduced gradually.

items.q: How many new foods at once?
items.a: At first, introduce new foods gradually so you can spot any reactions more easily.
Not necessarily. Match texture to age and skills: purees, but also soft textures for self-feeding exploration.

items.q: How much should baby eat at first?
items.a: Amounts vary a lot. Early on the goal is exploring tastes and textures, not a set quantity.

items.q: Does milk still matter after starting solids?
items.a: Yes. Early in weaning, breast milk or formula keeps playing a major role in nutrition.

items.q: How often to offer solid food?
items.a: Meal frequency grows gradually with age, development and appetite.
Allergenic foods can be introduced during weaning in safe, age-appropriate forms. With risk factors, talk to your pediatrician.

items.q: What to avoid at the start?
items.a: Avoid choking hazards and foods unsuitable for infants, plus certain foods and drinks in the first year.
Baby eats only under constant supervision, seated correctly, with age-appropriate shapes and textures.
Yes, refusal is common at first. Several exposures are sometimes needed before a new taste or texture is accepted.

items.q: Should I force my baby to eat?
items.a: No. Respect hunger and fullness cues and avoid pressuring.

items.q: Can I use salt and sugar?
items.a: It's best not to get baby used to salty or sugary foods. Plain foods let them discover natural tastes.
With solids, water can be offered in suitable amounts without replacing milk as the main nutrition at this stage.

items.q: What if baby reacts to a new food?
items.a: Stop the suspect food and watch symptoms. For severe reactions (trouble breathing, face/lip swelling, poor condition) seek emergency care.

cookies.title: Cookie policy

sections.h: 1. What are cookies and local storage?
sections.p: Cookies are small text files saved by your browser. Local storage (localStorage) keeps data right in your browser and remembers your preferences between visits.
Strictly what's needed: your login token (if you sign in), the interface language, and your banner choice. No tracking, analytics or advertising cookies.
Login tokens expire in 7 days. Language and cookie choice stay until you clear them in your browser.
You can delete site data anytime in browser settings. Without local storage login won't work, but recipes stay freely visible.
Data questions — reach us from the profile page or the contact form.
